options.text: At run time, on the values passed to it
At compile time, on tokens, before names are resolved and types are checked
At compile time, after type checking, so it can see the types of its arguments
At link time

questions.why:
Expansion happens between lexing and parsing. A macro sees a stream of tokens and produces a stream of tokens; the rest of the compiler then runs on the output.

C is the answer people want to be true, and its falsity explains most macro frustration. A macro cannot ask whether its argument implements Display, cannot look up the definition of a type you named, and cannot see any value. It matches shapes. That is why #[derive(Serialize)] generates code that calls trait methods rather than inspecting anything.

questions.stem:
What does this print?

rust
macro_rules! square { ($x:expr) => { $x * $x }; }
println!("{}", square!(3 + 1));

options.text: 7, because the expansion is 3 + 1 * 3 + 1
It does not compile, because the macro needs parentheses

questions.why:
1. Once 3 + 1 has matched an expr fragment it is a parsed expression node,

one opaque unit, so substituting it cannot change how anything around it groups.

A is the C answer, and it is correct in C: #define SQUARE(x) x * x really does expand to 3 + 1 * 3 + 1, which is 7, and every C programmer learns to write ((x) * (x)). Rust needs no defensive parentheses because it substitutes syntax trees rather than text.

questions.stem: Which of these can a macro do that a function cannot? Choose all that apply.

options.text: Take a different number of arguments at different call sites
Take a type as an argument
Define a new struct or impl
Recover the source text of its argument
Return different types at different call sites

questions.why:
A, B, C and D are the four capabilities that justify the feature, and if your problem is none of them you want a function or a generic.

E is the trap. A generic function already does this: fn first<T>(v: &[T]) -> &T returns whatever T is, and "3".parse::<u8>() is decided by the call site. Returning a call-site-dependent type is exactly what generics are for, and using a macro to get it is choosing a worse tool.

questions.stem:
Does this compile?

rust
macro_rules! bump { () => { count += 1; }; }

let mut count = 0;
bump!();

options.text: Yes, because count is in scope at the call site
No: error[E0425]: cannot find value count in this scope
Yes, but count stays 0
No, because a macro cannot contain an assignment

questions.why:
This is hygiene. Identifiers written inside a macro body are resolved where the macro was defined, not where it was called, so the macro's count and yours are different identifiers that happen to be spelled the same.

C is the tempting wrong answer because it assumes the macro quietly operates on some other count. It does not. There is no other count, and the compiler says so rather than guessing. That refusal is the entire safety property.

questions.stem: Which of these does hygiene protect? Choose all that apply.

options.text: A local variable the macro declares cannot shadow one at the call site
A local at the call site cannot be captured by a name the macro wrote
A type named in the macro body always means what it meant at the definition site
A function called by the macro body always resolves to the definition site's crate

questions.why:
macro_rules! hygiene covers local variables and lifetimes, which is A and B.

C and D are the ones people assume and they are false, which is a real hazard. A macro body naming Vec gets whatever Vec means at the call site, so a caller with struct Vec; in scope breaks your macro. That is why exported macros write ::std::vec::Vec and $crate::helper in full rather than bare paths.

questions.stem:
Which fragment specifier should $t be here?

rust
macro_rules! zeroed { ($t:???) => { <$t>::default() }; }
zeroed!(Vec<u8>);

options.text: expr
ty
ident
tt

questions.why:
<$t>::default() uses the fragment in type position, so it must be matched as a type. The rule is to choose for the role the fragment plays in the output, not for what the caller happens to type.

C is wrong for a specific and useful reason: Vec<u8> is not one identifier, it is four tokens. A is the common mistake and produces expected type, found expression, pointing at a line inside the macro that the reader never wrote. D would match, since tt matches nearly anything, but only the first token tree, so it would capture Vec and choke on <.

questions.stem: What does $(,)? add to a matcher like ($($x:expr),* $(,)?)?

options.text: It makes the comma separator optional between arguments
It allows one optional trailing comma after the last argument
It allows the macro to be called with no arguments
Nothing; it is a formatting convention

questions.why:
$( ... )? means zero or one occurrence, so $(,)? permits a single trailing comma. Without it, labels!["a", "b",] is a syntax error while labels!["a", "b"] is fine. That is an inconsistency rustfmt will happily create for you when a list wraps onto several lines.

C is already handled by the *, which allows zero repetitions. Put $(,)? on every list-shaped macro you write; vec! has it.

options.text: * separates with commas, + separates with plus signs
* allows zero repetitions, + requires at least one
+ is for the transcriber, * for the matcher
None; they are interchangeable

questions.why: The separator is whatever you write before the * or +; the sigil itself only says how many repetitions are allowed. + requiring at least one is genuinely useful: an enum-generating macro should use + so that named_enum!(Empty {}) is rejected at the call site rather than producing an enum nobody can construct.

options.text: Yes
No, because $x is used outside a repetition
No, because ident cannot be a receiver
Yes, but it only pushes the first argument

questions.why:
error: variable 'x' is still repeating at this depth. $x was bound inside a repetition, so every use of it must also be inside one: $( $v.push($x); )*.

D is the plausible-sounding guess and it is worth knowing why it is wrong. The compiler will not silently pick one match out of several; depth mismatches are errors, not defaults. The mirror-image error, wrapping something in $( )* that mentions no metavariable, is attempted to repeat an expression containing no syntax variables, since the compiler would have no idea how many times to repeat it.

questions.stem: A recursive macro hits error: recursion limit reached while expanding. What are reasonable responses? Choose all that apply.

options.text: Rewrite the macro as a procedural macro
Nothing; the code is wrong and cannot work
Ask whether the recursion should have been a $(...)* repetition or an ordinary loop
Raise it with #![recursion_limit = "256"] if the recursion is genuinely that deep

questions.why:
The default limit is 128 nested expansions. D is the honest fix when you really do need the depth, since long token-munching macros hit it legitimately.

C is the better first question. Expansion happens before everything else, so deep recursion is compile-time cost with nothing to show for it at run time, and most macros that recurse deeply were trying to do something a repetition or a plain function loop does better and faster.

options.text: At the crate root, regardless of which module defines it
In the module that defines it, made public
In every module of the crate
In the prelude of any crate that depends on yours

questions.why:
It lifts the macro to the crate root, so a macro defined in mod internal is imported as use my_crate::retry;, because the module it lives in is not part of its path. That surprises everybody exactly once.

B is the reasonable expectation from how pub works everywhere else, and it is wrong because macros are resolved during expansion, before the module tree matters. The related tool is $crate, a metavariable expanding to the defining crate's root: without it, a macro that calls a helper works in its own crate and breaks in every other one.

questions.stem: Which is the better tool for "the same logic over i32, i64 and u8"?

options.text: A macro_rules! macro taking $t:ty
A generic function with a trait bound
A procedural macro
Three copies of the function

questions.why:
A generic. It is a real function with a real signature, so rust-analyzer can complete it, the debugger can step into it, errors point at your source, and monomorphisation makes it exactly as fast.

A works and is the most common unnecessary macro in the wild. The test to apply: if a function or a generic can do it, the macro is a worse function or a worse generic. Macros earn their place when they generate items, take a variable number of arguments, or need the name of something as well as the thing.

questions.stem: What does a procedural macro receive and return?

options.text: A syntax tree, and a syntax tree
A TokenStream, and a TokenStream
The values of its arguments, evaluated at compile time
A string of source text

questions.why:
Tokens in, tokens out, and no type information whatsoever. A derive macro cannot look up the definition of a type you named in a field.

A is close enough to be misleading. Nobody manipulates a raw TokenStream by hand: syn parses one into a syntax tree and quote! builds a new one from a template. But that tree is syn's, built from tokens, and not the compiler's. The compiler's does not exist yet.

questions.stem: Which of these are true of procedural macros? Choose all that apply.

options.text: They must live in their own crate with proc-macro = true
They cannot be used in the crate that defines them
They can run arbitrary code at compile time, including reading files
They can inspect the types of the code they are attached to

questions.why:
A and B follow from the same fact: a proc-macro crate is compiled for the host and linked into the compiler, not into your program, so it has to be built first and separately.

C is why sqlx::query! can check your SQL against a live database at compile time, and why a proc macro is code you are choosing to trust.

D is the recurring wish and it is false. #[derive(Serialize)] on a struct sees the tokens of that struct and nothing else; it cannot find out what any field's type actually is, which is why the generated code calls trait methods and lets normal resolution sort it out later.

questions.stem: A #[derive] produces a confusing error. What is the fastest way to see what it generated?

options.text: Read the macro's source in the dependency
cargo expand
cargo build --verbose
Add println! calls to the macro

questions.why:
cargo expand prints your crate with every macro expanded, #[derive] output included, as ordinary readable Rust.

A is the instinct and it is the slow path: reading a macro means simulating expansion in your head, and syn-based derives are thousands of lines. D cannot work at all: a proc macro runs in the compiler, so its output goes to the compiler's stdout rather than your program's.

The habit: when a macro misbehaves, do not read the macro. Read what it produced, fix the ordinary bug you find there, then work backwards to the line of the transcriber that emitted it.
